summary: Earth Shield is an interactive 3D globe that brings two NASA data streams together in one view: natural hazards happening on Earth right now (wildfires, storms, icebergs) from NASA EONET, and every asteroid passing close to Earth this week from NASA NeoWs. Users can pick any real asteroid, drop it anywhere on the planet, and see what an impact would mean: damage zones on the globe, explosion energy with an uncertainty range, crater size, earthquake magnitude and a tsunami estimate for ocean impacts. The energy is compared with Hiroshima, Chelyabinsk, Tunguska and the dinosaur-killing Chicxulub impact. A "Could we stop it?" planner, based on real results from NASA's 2022 DART mission, shows how many DART-class spacecraft would be needed to deflect the asteroid for a chosen warning time, or whether evacuation would be the only option. Earth Shield turns planetary defense into something anyone can understand in a minute: the earlier we find asteroids, the more options we have.

FULL DISCLOSURE: AI, TOOLS AND RESOURCES USED

ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
- Claude (Anthropic), model Claude Opus 5.5, used through the Claude Code desktop app. It built almost the whole project:
- proposed the project ideas (I chose to combine two of them);
- wrote all of the code (HTML, CSS, JavaScript), the visual design, the logo icon and all interface text;
- chose the scientific formulas from the published sources below and implemented them;
- tested the site in a browser, fixed bugs, and published it to GitHub;
- wrote the README and this submission text;
- wrote the demo video script and captions, recorded the video automatically and edited it.
- Higgsfield AI (Seed Audio text-to-speech) was tried for the video narration. Only one test line was generated, and it is NOT used in the final video.

WHAT I DID MYSELF
- Chose the idea and directed the work: asked for features, simpler wording, the site language, the video and the voice.
- Reviewed and tried the site, reported problems and decided what to keep.
- Registered for a NASA API key and approved publishing the project.

NASA DATA AND IMAGERY
- NASA EONET v3 API: natural events (live).
- NASA NeoWs API: near-Earth asteroid close approaches (live, with a personal api.nasa.gov key).
- NASA Blue Marble Earth image (globe texture, also used to detect land or ocean at the impact point), loaded from the three-globe example images.
- Published results of NASA's DART mission (2022): spacecraft mass, impact speed and momentum-enhancement factor.
- No data, images or results shown in the app were generated by AI.

SCIENTIFIC SOURCES
- Collins, Melosh & Marcus (2005), Earth Impact Effects Program: crater size, earthquake magnitude, tsunami height.
- Glasstone & Dolan (1977), The Effects of Nuclear Weapons: blast and heat ranges.
- Cheng et al. (2023), Nature 616, 457-460: DART momentum transfer (beta about 3.6).
- Commonly cited energy values: Hiroshima about 15 kt, Chelyabinsk about 500 kt, Tunguska about 10-15 Mt (12 Mt used), Chicxulub about 100 million Mt.

OPEN-SOURCE SOFTWARE AND SERVICES
- globe.gl 2.27.2 (includes three.js) for the 3D globe, loaded from the jsDelivr CDN.
- three-globe 2.31.0 example images: Earth texture, topology bump map and night-sky background.
- Google Fonts: Sora, IBM Plex Sans, IBM Plex Mono.
- GitHub (code repository) and GitHub Pages (hosting).

TOOLS USED TO BUILD AND MAKE THE VIDEO
- Claude Code desktop app, including its built-in browser for testing.
- Python (local web server), Node.js, git and the GitHub CLI.
- Playwright with Google Chrome to record the demo video automatically.
- ffmpeg (ffmpeg-static) to encode the video and mix the audio.
- macOS text-to-speech, voice "Daniel", for the narration.
dataRefs: NASA EONET - Earth Observatory Natural Event Tracker
projectRefs: Earth Impact Effects Program - Collins, Melosh & Marcus (2005)
